old: Across three model scales, two RL objectives, and harder task constructions, rehearsing verified successes raises how often a policy succeeds, and rehearsing them uniformly is what preserves how many ways it can succeed.

old: Overall, our findings shed light on solution mode collapse and suggest that incorporating mode replay as part of RLVR post-training can lead to both increased diversity of solutions and improved model performance.
new: Together, these studies connect how successful alternatives are measured, why reward-driven learning concentrates them, and when retaining them helps a policy cope with changed requirements.

old: For each domain, we provide a verifier that evaluates whether a solution is correct and which solution mode a solution belongs to. old: measuring the joint probability of different solution modes given two correct responses. A \pmd{} of zero thus implies every correct answer belongs to the same solution mode, and an even spread over $m$ yields a \pmd{} of $1-1/m$, e.g., if answers spread evenly across two possible solution modes, then the \pmd{} is $1/2$. We note that when infinite solution modes are possible, the maximum \pmd{} converges to 1, and that when the model outputs no correct solutions, we cannot calculate the metric. We only calculate \pmd{} when models yield at least 30 correct solutions for a specific problem, to avoid excessively noisy measurements.

We construct \mb{} so that tasks can be made more or less challenging, which helps prevent saturation.

For each domain, we include 5 independent difficulty levels,  e.g. for our \texttt{Graph} domain we allow more hidden vertices, and for \texttt{Countdown} we give the model more operands. Each difficulty level holds constant (1) our definition of mode, (2) our approximate distribution of modes, (3) our verifier constant, and (4) the sample size of 384 train and 128 test problems.

To ensure (2) holds, and moreover, that the problems sample are in fact more challenging, we fit each level with consideration to \texttt{pass@1} and \texttt{pass@8} of a reference model, e.g. Level 4 was tuned such that a Qwen2.5-Instruct-7B model has the same \texttt{pass@1} and \texttt{pass@8} scores as a Qwen2.5-Instruct-0.5B on Level 1.



LMs with a higher parameter count generally have higher \texttt{pass@8} and can solve more problems. Yet, in Fig. \ref{fig:levels}, for our harder problems, we find that solution mode diversity declines, even as our underlying mode count per level remains stable. This is most noticeable when frontier models are evaluated. Even though correctness is saturated, we are able to use  \pmd{} to isolate solution mode collapse (App.~\ref{app:hosted-concentration}), and this phenomena happen across \mb{}. Frontier models answer $\MDfrontierpass$ of questions from level 1-3 correctly, but their mean \pmd{}  is $\MDfrontierpmdmean{}$, which is below the $\MDsmallbestpmd{}$ of a 1.5B model that answers $\MDsmallbestpassall$ of its own prompts.

We construct five levels per domain by increasing structural difficulty, such as hiding more vertices in \texttt{Graph} or adding operands in \texttt{Countdown}. Each level retains the verifier, canonicalizer, and definition of a mode, with 384 training and 128 test problems. Valid-mode count distributions can differ across the evaluated test sets. Levels 3--5 calibrate larger models against the Level-1 Qwen2.5-0.5B reference using \texttt{pass@1} and \texttt{pass@8} tolerances; Level-4 \texttt{MathIR} does not meet this criterion (App.~\ref{app:data-levels}).

Fig.~\ref{fig:levels} shows that correct-mode diversity can decline across levels even for highly accurate models. These comparisons combine changes in task structure and test population. Across Levels 1--3, frontier models answer $\MDfrontierpass$ of questions correctly, but their mean \pmd{} is $\MDfrontierpmdmean{}$, below the $\MDsmallbestpmd{}$ of a 1.5B model that answers $\MDsmallbestpassall$ of its own prompts (App.~\ref{app:hosted-concentration}).

Changing the binary-reward estimator alone does not change the trajectory of this concentration, as the following result makes precise.

old: We test three claims: RLVR concentrates correct responses onto fewer modes; verified replay improves accuracy and diversity; and balancing replay across modes contributes additional diversity. We then examine harder task levels and compare replay with anchoring to the initial policy.
new: We first test whether RLVR concentrates correct responses, then whether replay and equal weighting preserve alternatives. We examine harder task levels, compare replay with anchoring to the initial policy, and test whether retained solutions remain useful after requirements change.
